name: LM5109BMAX_NOPB
title: LM5109B: 90 V, 1 A peak half-bridge gate driver for two N-channel MOSFETs
summary: The LM5109B drives the gates of a high-side and a low-side N-channel MOSFET, as in a half bridge or a synchronous buck stage. Each output has its own logic input with TTL/CMOS levels, sources and sinks 1 A peak, and the floating high-side stage runs on a bootstrap supply up to 108 V DC with its switch node at up to 90 V; the bootstrap diode is external. Both the VDD rail and the bootstrap rail carry undervoltage lockout. It comes in 8-pin SOIC (D) and 8-pin WSON (NGT) with an exposed pad; LM5109BMAX/NOPB is the SOIC on a 2500-piece reel.

circuits.title: Simplified application
circuits.description: The driver runs a half bridge of two N-channel MOSFETs between VIN and ground; the switch node between them is the output to the load. VCC feeds VDD directly, bypassed by C2 to ground, and also charges the bootstrap capacitor C1 through RBoot and DBoot whenever the lower switch pulls HS low. C1 then supplies the high-side driver from HB to HS. HI and LI are the two logic inputs.

circuits.title: Half-bridge converter driven from a PWM controller
circuits.description: Two outputs of a PWM controller, OUT1 and OUT2, drive HI and LI; the controller and the driver share the VCC rail. The driver switches a half bridge of two N-channel MOSFETs across VIN. The switch node feeds the primary of transformer T1, whose other end sits at the midpoint of two capacitors split across VIN and ground; the secondary goes to the secondary-side circuit. Each gate is fed through its own RGATE, and an optional diode across each RGATE, cathode at the driver, takes the gate down faster at turn-off. RBOOT and DBOOT charge the 0.1 µF CBOOT from VCC; 1.0 µF bypasses VDD. The design example for this circuit runs at VDD = 10 V and 500 kHz with RBOOT = 2.2 Ω, RGATE = 4.7 Ω and CSD19534KCS MOSFETs.

operation.text: Two independent channels: LI controls LO, referred to VSS, and HI controls HO, referred to the floating HS node. A level shifter carries the HI signal up to the high-side stage at high speed and low power while keeping its delay matched to the low side. The high side is powered from a bootstrap capacitor between HB and HS, which an external high-voltage diode charges; HB may reach 108 V. Typical uses named: current-fed push-pull, half- and full-bridge, two-switch forward and active-clamp topologies, synchronous buck stages and solid-state motor drives.

Separate undervoltage lockouts watch VDD and the bootstrap voltage HB–HS, each with hysteresis so the outputs do not chatter as a supply wanders. Until VDD rises past VDDR (6.7 V typ) both HO and LO stay low whatever the inputs. Once running, VDD has to fall below VDDR – VDDH before both outputs are forced low. An undervoltage on HB–HS turns off only HO; LO keeps following LI (Tables 1 and 2).
Both outputs have low resistance, fast edges and 1 A peak drive. The low-side stage is referred to VSS, the high-side stage to HS.

The part is either in UVLO or in normal mode. In normal mode, with VDD and HB–HS both above their thresholds, each output follows its own input (Table 3). The inputs have internal pulldowns (200 kΩ typ), so a floating input gives a low output.

The lower MOSFET's body diode clamps HS, yet board resistance and inductance can still ring it several volts negative. This is allowed when three things hold. HO must not go more than 0.3 V below HS, nor LO below VSS, or parasitic transistors conduct heavy current from HB and can destroy the part; a Schottky diode right at the pins from HO to HS, or from LO to ground, guards against it. HB–HS must stay at 15 V or less, so with HS spiking to –5 V, VDD should be held to 10 V. And low-ESR capacitors must sit at the pins across HB–HS and across VDD–VSS, since series inductance with them rings the pins under the large peak output currents.

Size CBoot so that one cycle's charge (gate charge plus leakage and quiescent draw) does not pull HB–HS below the HB falling threshold, then use a good deal more; the 10 V, 500 kHz example needs 7.6 nF and uses 100 nF placed at HB and HS. The local VDD capacitor is about ten times CBoot, 1 µF in the example. Both are X7R ceramics rated at twice the highest VDD, allowing for capacitance lost under DC bias and for long-term reliability.

VDD recharges CBoot through the external diode every time the low-side MOSFET is on. The charging pulses are large, so the diode's forward drop and its reverse recovery both add to the driver circuit's losses; application note AN-1317 (SNVA083) covers diode choice. RBoot, 2 Ω to 10 Ω depending on the diode, limits the diode's inrush current and slows the rise of HB–HS each cycle, which matters most when HS swings far negative. With 2.2 Ω the peak diode current is about 4 A.

An external RGATE in each gate lead damps ringing from stray inductance and capacitance and caps the peak gate current; with 4.7 Ω, 2.2 Ω inside the MOSFET and 9 V across, the HO peak pullup current comes to 0.48 A. Where a fast turn-off is needed, a diode across RGATE, pointing back toward the driver, bypasses the resistor when the gate is pulled down.

VDD runs from 8 V to 14 V. The VDD UVLO sets the floor; the ceiling leaves 4 V below the 18 V absolute maximum for spikes. Running near 8 V, ripple on the bias supply must stay smaller than VDDH or the part drops into lockout. Bypass VDD to ground right at the part with two surface-mount ceramics: 100 nF for high-frequency current and a second of 220 nF to 10 µF for bias. HO draws its current pulses from HB, so put 22 nF to 220 nF from HB to HS.

Put low-ESR, low-ESL capacitors close to the IC from VDD to VSS and from HB to HS: they deliver the peak currents when the MOSFETs turn on. A low-ESR electrolytic and a good ceramic from the upper MOSFET's drain to ground keep drain transients down. Keep the inductance from the upper MOSFET's source to the lower MOSFET's drain small, to limit negative spikes on HS. Keep the gate charge and discharge loops tight by putting the driver next to the MOSFETs. The second loop to shrink is the bootstrap recharge path: bootstrap capacitor, bootstrap diode, ground-referred VDD capacitor and lower MOSFET body diode, which carries short, high current pulses every cycle. On the WSON, solder the exposed pad to a ground plane that extends beyond the package.
